lines: Chaining, open addressing, Swiss Tables — every single one of them quietly assumed the table already had room.
Not one of them ever said what happens the moment it doesn't.
That's the whole question this topic finally answers.
Here's the simplest possible answer, and it's the same move a growable array already makes.
When the table's full, allocate one twice the size, and rehash every single existing entry into it, right then, all at once.
Averaged over many inserts, that's still cheap. But somebody has to actually sit through the one insert where all of that happens.
Here's a row of ordinary inserts, and one of them is the one that triggers that rehash.
Before I show you the real number, predict it: how does that one insert's cost compare to its neighbors?
answer: Proportional to the whole table's current size — nowhere close to its neighbors.
That insert has to rehash every existing entry before it can even finish. The average cost was always fine. This one insert is not.

lines: Here's a real production answer, built completely differently.
Keep the old table exactly as it is, and start a new one beside it, both live at the same time.
Instead of pausing to move everything at once, move it gradually, a little at a time.
There's a migration pointer sitting between those two tables right now.
Predict it: what actually makes that pointer move forward?
answer: It's piggybacked on every ordinary lookup or insert that touches the table — no separate thread, nothing running in the background.
It rides along on work the table was already doing. No thread, no scheduler, no separate cost to account for.

lines: Here's the bound, and it's a real one, not a hand-wave.
Each operation moves only a fixed, small number of buckets, capped, every single time.
The table keeps growing, sure — but no single operation ever pays for the whole migration. Just its own small, fixed share.
I want to be honest about this: neither strategy here is free.
Incremental migration's smoother latency comes at a real cost — both tables stay live, roughly doubling peak memory, for as long as the migration takes.
Not for one insert. For every single operation until the migration finally finishes.
Same key sequence into both tables, measured, not assumed.
Watch the difference: one strategy pays for the resize in a single tall spike. The other spreads the exact same total work into many small, bounded steps.
Same final table. Same total work. A completely different schedule for who pays, and when.
